nullify

NUHL-uh-fy -- from Latin nullus ('none') + -ficare ('to make'). · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To nullify is to make legally void or invalid.

A clerical error on the birth certificate was enough to nullify the entire passport application.

Example

After discovering that one juror had lied about knowing the defendant, the judge has no choice but to nullify the entire verdict.

To nullify the verdict is to make it legally void, as if it had never existed at all.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

invalidate: To invalidate something is to strip it of legal force, usually by pointing to a flaw -- a missing signature, an expired date. It sits very close to nullify in strength, but nullify is the classic courtroom word for wiping out an entire law, contract, or election result.

annul: To annul is to declare a formal union or act legally void from the very start, and in everyday use it belongs almost entirely to marriage. Nullify ranges much more widely: courts, referees, and lawmakers can nullify contracts, goals, and laws alike.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

ratify: to formally approve and make valid

uphold: to confirm or support a decision as valid

Where it sits · how much gets legally wiped out

revoke → nullify → abolish

revoke vs. nullify: Revoke is often narrower than nullify -- you revoke a specific privilege, like a license or invitation, while nullify can wipe out an entire agreement, election, or law all at once.

abolish vs. nullify: Abolish goes even further than nullify -- a court may nullify one contract or one election result, but to abolish something, like slavery or an unjust tax, is to wipe the entire practice out of existence for good.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — null-: none, nothing (Latin (nullus))

suffix — -ify: to make, cause to become (Latin (-ficare))

Put it together: Nullify comes from Latin nullus ('none') plus -ficare ('to make') -- so to nullify something is literally to 'make it nothing,' stripping it of any legal force as though it had never existed.

Use the root in a new word: null: The league voted to annul the results of Saturday's match.

Word Choice

Nullify is most common in legal, political, and sports contexts -- courts nullify laws, referees nullify goals, and voters can nullify an election result through a formal challenge.
